title: PSCI 1104 — Real Finding or Good Story?

lines.t: Somebody claims X causes Y. Should you believe them? That is the entire course. Fourteen units, seven debates, and one question asked over and over.
And once you see it that way the readings stop being about Kansas or welfare or crime. They become fourteen worked examples of the same problem.
So this is the machinery. Theory, measurement, causality, design, sampling, inference — then the debates, then the exam frames, then a self-test.

The grade, quickly, so you know what you are aiming at. The final is thirty-five percent, cumulative, December seventeenth. The midterm is thirty, in class, October fifteenth. Six quizzes are five percent each. Attendance on Top Hat is the last five.
And the quizzes have a structure worth knowing.

Each one has a take-home part posted at nine in the morning the day before, due before class, plus an in-class part. So the take-home is where you build the notes you will want later. Do not throw them away.
Unit one. Theory-driven research.

Science is not a pile of facts, it is a loop. You have a hunch about why something happens, you turn it into a prediction that could turn out wrong, you collect evidence, and you find out. The part that makes it science is that the prediction can lose.
Theory versus hypothesis. What is the difference?

A theory is the general explanation of why X causes Y, and it has to apply beyond the case in front of you. Voting is partly social — people vote to avoid looking like a shirker. That is a theory. The hypothesis is one specific testable prediction that follows from it.
Give me the matching hypothesis.
Households told their neighbours will see their turnout record will vote at higher rates than households that are not told. Two variables, a direction, a unit of analysis, and a way to lose.
Falsifiability.
If no possible evidence could prove you wrong, you are not doing science. Politics is complicated is unfalsifiable. It sounds wise and it forbids nothing.
And empirical versus normative, which people mix up constantly.

Empirical is what is, settled by evidence. Normative is what ought to be, settled by values. Turnout is sixty percent, versus turnout should be higher. Those are different kinds of sentence and no amount of data settles the second one.
Now the first reading of the semester, which is my favourite. Where numbers come from.
Fisman, Gelman and Stephenson trace famous statistics back to their sources and find that most of them have none.
The body heat one.

You lose eighty percent of your body heat through your head. It comes from a nineteen fifties military study where the subjects wore Arctic suits covering everything except the head. The real figure is about ten percent.
The corruption ones.

Bribery costs one trillion dollars a year is the midpoint of a six hundred billion to one point seven trillion range, taken from a handful of old surveys. Collapsing a range to its midpoint deletes the uncertainty, which was the most honest part of the estimate.
And the two point six trillion figure.
That traces to a one-sentence bullet in an advocacy brief that cited no source. Then the heads of the U N and the O E C D repeated it, and after that everybody cited them.
Which is the thing with a name.
Statistics laundering. A shaky figure gets repeated by a respectable body, and then the respectable body becomes the citation.
Their four rules. Say them, because these are quiz-friendly.

One, trace the number to its original source, not to whoever cited it. Studies have shown and it has been estimated are red flags. Two, watch for statistics laundering. Three, a Harvard professor's guess is not a Harvard estimate. Four, beware the broken telephone effect — ranges collapse to points, caveats fall off, and narrow findings get generalised.

lines.chapter: Measurement, and why it decides Kansas
lines.t: Unit two. Measurement. You told me this is where most political arguments actually go wrong.
It is. You cannot test a claim about the working class until you say exactly who counts. And this is where the course spends the most time.
Conceptual versus operational definition.

Conceptual says what you mean, in words. Working class means people whose income depends on wages rather than assets or credentials. Operational is the exact recipe — specific enough that a stranger would produce the same numbers. Working class means white respondents with no four-year college degree.
Validity and reliability. This is the dartboard.

Validity asks whether you are measuring the thing you claim to measure. That is a bias problem. Reliability asks whether the same procedure gives the same answer when repeated. That is a consistency problem.
And the dangerous box is which one?

Reliable but not valid. Consistently wrong. Self-reported turnout is the example — people answer the same way every time, and they overreport. And here is the part that matters: more data never fixes a validity problem. A bigger sample of a biased measure is a more precise wrong answer.
Levels of measurement, and the classic trap.

Nominal names categories with no order — party, religion, state. You may compute a mode and percentages. Ordinal ranks them but the gaps are not equal — strongly agree through strongly disagree. Mode and median only. Interval or ratio are real numbers with equal gaps — turnout, income, age. Everything is available.
So the trap.

You cannot take a mean of a nominal variable. The average religion is nonsense. And an ordinal variable gets a median, not a mean, because the distance from agree to strongly agree is not a known quantity.
Now Kansas, because this is where measurement stops being abstract.

Thomas Frank argues that white working-class voters abandoned the Democrats because culture outweighs economics. His headline evidence is that the poorest county in America went for Bush by over seventy-five percent.
And Bartels asks a different question.

He asks the measurement question. Who is the working class? Change the operational definition and the answer flips. Fourteen elections of American National Election Studies data, nineteen fifty-two to two thousand four.
Give me the three numbers.

Among white non-college voters in two thousand four, forty percent had family incomes over sixty thousand dollars, and more than half described themselves as middle class. So no college degree is a poor operationalisation of working class. Bush's margin among the bottom third by income of that group was under two points. And define working class by income instead, and the poorest white voters moved toward the Democrats.
So the verdict on Frank.

He never fixed his definition, so his thesis was never testable. And by twenty twenty, Ruffini finds the income divide has nearly vanished — Clinton won the lowest earners by thirty-one points in ninety-six while Dole won the highest by sixteen, a forty-seven point spread, against roughly eight points in twenty twenty.

lines.chapter: Describing data, and the ecological fallacy
lines.t: Unit three. Before you explain anything, you describe it.
Three questions about any variable. Where is the middle, how spread out is it, and is it lopsided.
Mean, median or mode — how do I choose?

Skew decides. Income is the classic right-skewed variable: a handful of very rich people drag the mean far above the median. Which is why average income flatters and median income describes. The mean always sits toward the tail.
Standard deviation, in words.
The typical distance of a case from the mean. A small standard deviation means the cases are bunched together.
And now the fallacy that is worth points on every exam.

The ecological fallacy. Inferring something about individuals from data about groups. Poor counties voted for Bush, therefore poor people voted for Bush — that does not follow. The unit of analysis was the county, not the person.
Where does it show up on the syllabus?

Twice. In Frank's red-state map. And in Messerli's chocolate study, which correlates national chocolate consumption with national Nobel counts and never observes a single laureate eating anything at all.
Unit four. The vocabulary you get tested on.
Independent variable X is the proposed cause. Dependent variable Y is the effect — it depends on X. The null hypothesis says there is no relationship between them, and that is what you actually test.
What can you do with the null?
Reject it, or fail to reject it. You never accept it. That phrasing is worth points on its own.
Antecedent versus intervening. Say this carefully, because they look identical on a diagram.

An antecedent variable comes before X and causes both X and Y. That makes the relationship spurious and it kills the claim. An intervening variable sits between X and Y and transmits the effect. That explains the claim and leaves it standing.
Same diagram, opposite verdict.
Exactly. Which is why it is a favourite exam distinction.
And the four ways students lose these points.

No variation in Y — asking why do people vote and then studying only voters. A definition rather than a claim — partisans are loyal to their party. A single case with nothing to compare it to. And no stated direction — education is related to turnout does not say which way.
Unit five. And you have told me this is the single most testable thing in the course.
It is. Kellstedt and Whitten give you four questions to run any causal claim through. Answer them yes, no, or maybe. One confident no kills the claim.
In order.

One. Is there a credible causal mechanism connecting X to Y? Two. Can we rule out that Y causes X? Three. Is there covariation — do they actually move together? Four. Have we controlled for confounding variables Z?
And which one do public arguments clear?
Hurdle three. And they stop there. Chocolate and Nobel prizes clears hurdle three and fails the other three.
Why is random assignment so powerful?
Because it clears hurdles two and four at once. The researcher sets X, so Y cannot have caused it. And randomisation balances every confounder in expectation — including the ones nobody thought of.
Now define cause, properly.
Bueno de Mesquita and Fowler define it with a counterfactual. X caused Y for a case if Y would have been different had X been different, with everything else held fixed.
And that definition creates a problem.

The fundamental problem of causal inference. For each case there are two potential outcomes — what happens if treated, and what happens if not. You only ever observe one of them. The counterfactual is never seen.
So what is every research method actually doing?
Constructing a believable stand-in for the missing counterfactual. That stand-in is your control group. Say that sentence in an exam and you have shown you understand the whole field.
Four things people get wrong about causes.

There is no such thing as the cause — outcomes have many, and every causal claim is relative to a stated counterfactual. A single counterexample does not refute a causal claim, because causation here is about averages, not certainties. Causes precede effects. And a mechanism is not strictly required for an effect to be real.
One more, which people forget entirely. Can there be causation without correlation?
Yes. If the effect runs in opposite directions for different groups, or if people compensate for it, the net correlation can be zero while the causal effect is real.
Unit six. The distinction that shows up every single semester.

Random sampling is not random assignment. Sampling picks who is in your study, and it buys external validity — generalisability. Assignment decides who gets the treatment, and it buys internal validity — causal confidence.
And most studies have?
Exactly one. A national survey has the first and not the second. A lab experiment on sixty undergraduates has the second and not the first.
Threats to internal validity. Give me the list.

History — something else happens between pretest and posttest and gets credited to your treatment. Maturation — subjects change on their own. Testing — taking the pretest changes the posttest. Instrumentation — the measure or the coder drifts. Regression to the mean — extreme cases drift back toward average by themselves. Selection bias — the groups differed beforehand. Attrition — people drop out non-randomly. Demand effects — subjects behave differently because they know they are watched. And diffusion — the control group gets the treatment anyway.
Which is the biggest?
Selection bias, in observational work, by a distance.
And the named designs.

The classical randomised design has a pretest and posttest for both groups. The posttest-only control group design drops the pretest specifically to avoid testing effects. The Solomon four-group design combines both so the testing effect can be isolated rather than dodged.
Rank the design menu.

On internal validity, weakest to strongest: case study, cross-sectional survey, panel, quasi-experiment, field experiment, lab experiment. External validity runs roughly the other way, which is the trade-off the whole unit is about.
Unit seven. And the flagship study.
Gerber, Green and Larimer, two thousand eight. A hundred and eighty thousand households, four escalating mailers, against a control group that turned out at twenty-nine point seven percent.
Give me the ladder.

Civic duty — a reminder that voting is a duty — plus one point eight points. Hawthorne — you are being studied — plus two point five. Self — here is your own voting record — plus four point nine. Neighbours — and we will show your record to the people on your street — plus eight point one.
And the conclusion.
Turnout is not driven by information. It is driven by being seen.
Why four treatments instead of one?
To identify the mechanism. A single mailer only shows that mail works. Each escalating step adds exactly one ingredient, and the size of the jump tells you what that ingredient is worth.
Put the effect in context.

Single mailings before this typically moved turnout less than one point. The eight-point effect rivals face-to-face canvassing, at one dollar ninety-three per vote for Neighbours against roughly twenty dollars a vote door to door. This experiment changed how American campaigns are run.
And the ethical objection, because you should be able to state it.
It worked by shaming people, using public records, without their consent, and it generated hundreds of angry phone calls to the researchers. A good exam answer names the effect and the cost.
Second experiment. Bertrand and Mullainathan.

About five thousand résumés to more than thirteen hundred job ads in sales, admin, clerical and customer service, Boston and Chicago, two thousand one to two thousand two. Names drawn from Massachusetts birth-certificate data to sound distinctively white or distinctively African-American.
The headline.

Nine point six five percent callback for white-sounding names against six point four five for Black-sounding names. A three point two point gap — fifty percent higher — worth about eight extra years of experience.
And the interaction, which is the part people miss.

Improving the résumé raised white callbacks by two point two nine points, and Black callbacks by only zero point five one, which was not statistically significant. The gap widens as qualifications improve.
Why does randomly assigning the name solve a problem no survey can?

Because employers see more about applicants than researchers do, so any observed gap in real hiring could be something unmeasured. Assigning the name to an otherwise identical résumé removes that possibility entirely.
So the exam question: why is this an experiment?

Three moves. The researcher manipulated the independent variable rather than observing it. Assignment was random, so the groups were equivalent beforehand on everything, measured or not. And outcomes were compared across groups, so the difference is the causal effect. Then say which hurdles it clears — two and four automatically, three by measurement, and one you still have to argue.
One more thing, on checking an experiment.

The balance table. Compare the groups on background characteristics before treatment — it is the check that randomisation worked. Gerber, Green and Larimer report one and the groups are statistically indistinguishable. If a study skips the balance table, ask why.
Unit eight. Because most political questions cannot be randomised.
You cannot assign someone a race, a region, or an income. So the fallback is controlled comparison — split the sample by the suspected confounder Z and look at the X–Y relationship inside each slice.
Three outcomes. What does each mean?

If the relationship holds inside every slice, Z was not doing the work and X survives. If it disappears in every slice, Z caused both and the relationship was spurious. And if it is strong in one slice and absent in another, that is an interaction — X matters, but only under certain conditions.
Run Kansas through it.

Uncontrolled, white non-college voters moved five point nine points Republican over fifty-two years. Control for region and it is entirely Southern: minus nineteen point seven in the South, minus one point zero outside it.
Fifty-two years, one point.
Nothing happened. And the South realigned over race, not culture-war economics.
The permanent limit of statistical control.

You can only control for variables you measured and thought of. Randomisation balances the ones you did not. That asymmetry is why an experiment on a small artificial question often beats a giant observational study on the real one — and it is the standard critique to deploy on any survey-based causal claim.
Now Leighley and Nagler, who show when not to control.

Two questions that look identical and are not. Are poor people underrepresented among voters? Do not control for anything — just compare shares. Controlling for age or education there would answer a different question.
And the second.
Is a poor person less likely to vote than an otherwise identical richer person? Now you must control, because income rises with age and young people vote less.
Their tool for the first question.

The representativeness ratio. A group's share of actual voters divided by its share of the citizen voting-age population. One point zero is parity. Above one is overrepresented, below one underrepresented.
And the punchline finding.

The bottom income fifth sat at zero point seven nine in nineteen seventy-two, and zero point seven nine in two thousand eight. Across thirty-six years of exploding economic inequality, it did not move.
And turnout itself.

Has not declined. Fifty-eight point four to sixty-five point five percent throughout, once you use citizens as the denominator. The apparent decline everyone cites is a denominator artifact — noncitizens grew from under two percent of the voting-age population to eight point four.
There is also a lovely methodological point about relative versus absolute measures.

College graduates went from twelve percent of adults in nineteen seventy-two to twenty-nine point four percent in two thousand eight. Measured in absolute categories, the least-educated group's representation looks like it collapsed — zero point seven nine down to zero point six two. Measured as the bottom third, it barely moved — zero point seven nine to zero point seven eight. Same data, two opposite stories, purely from the choice of measure.
Unit nine. The rule of thumb first.

Margin of error is approximately one divided by the square root of n. A thousand people gets you about plus or minus three points. To halve that you need four times the sample — four thousand people for one point six.
Does population size matter?
No. Fifteen hundred is as good for Nashville as it is for the United States, as long as the population is at least about a hundred times the sample. That surprises people every year.
Simple random sample. The exact wording matters.
Chosen so that every set of n individuals has an equal chance of being the sample. Note the wording — every individual has an equal chance is necessary but not sufficient.
Bias versus variability.
Bias is consistently off target, and it is fixed only by better design. Variability is scatter, and it is fixed by a bigger sample. Same dartboard as validity and reliability.
And the example that will be on a quiz.
Literary Digest, nineteen thirty-six. They mailed ten million ballots, got two point four million back, and confidently predicted Landon would beat Roosevelt. Roosevelt won in a landslide.
What went wrong?

Two things. Coverage error — the sample came from car registrations, phone books and magazine subscribers, all affluent in nineteen thirty-six. And voluntary response — respondents chose to mail it in. Gallup used a far smaller but better-designed sample and got it right.
The lesson in one line.
A huge sample cannot fix a biased design.
Unit ten, and the single idea of it.
The reported margin of error is the smallest error in a poll. It covers random sampling only. Everything else is bigger, and none of it shrinks when you interview more people.
List what it is not covering.

Coverage error — groups missing from the frame entirely, like cell-only households and non-English speakers. Nonresponse — the dominant problem today. Measurement and response bias — people misreport, and turnout overreporting is the classic. Question wording and order. Adjustment error, which is weighting. And likely-voter modelling.
Now Cohn's natural experiment, which is the best thing in this unit.

New York Times Upshot, twenty sixteen. Four outside pollsters were given the identical raw interviews from one Florida poll — eight hundred and sixty-seven of them. Same data, no sampling difference at all.
And the answers.

Spanned five points. From Clinton plus four to Trump plus one. Their implied electorates differed too — white share sixty-five to seventy percent, partisan balance from Democrat plus five to Republican plus one.
All of it from what?
Two judgment calls. How to weight the sample, and who counts as a likely voter. Cohn's conclusion is quotable: the reported margin of error does not even come close to capturing total survey error.
And Joshua Clinton's version, twenty twenty-four.
Sixteen defensible weighting schemes applied to one survey produced margins from Harris plus three point eight to Harris plus nine point four.
Hillygus's showcase.

Gallup in two thousand. Changes to the likely-voter model produced a nineteen point swing in the reported margin over a matter of days — none of it real movement. She argues the likely-voter screen is often the most consequential choice a pollster makes.
So what do you actually do with polls?
Average many rather than trusting one. But know the limit: averaging cancels random noise, not house effects. If every pollster misses cell-only households the same way, the average is just as wrong.
And one number that reframes the whole thing.
Only about five of every hundred contacted registered voters respond to a survey at all. So weighting is not a technical detail bolted on at the end. It is doing most of the work.
Units eleven through thirteen. Start with the normal curve.
You need it for one reason: it describes how sample statistics behave. Draw sample after sample from the same population and the sample means pile up in a bell shape centred on the truth.
The three numbers.
Sixty-eight, ninety-five, ninety-nine point seven. About sixty-eight percent of cases fall within one standard deviation of the mean, ninety-five within two, ninety-nine point seven within three.
Sampling distribution — and this is the one people misdefine.
It is not the distribution of your data. It is the distribution of a statistic across all the samples you could have drawn. It is normal, and it is centred on the true parameter.
Standard error.
The standard deviation of that sampling distribution — how much your estimate would bounce around from sample to sample. Bigger n, smaller standard error.
Confidence intervals. What does ninety-five percent confidence actually mean?

That the method captures the true value nineteen times in twenty across repeated sampling. It does not mean there is a ninety-five percent chance the truth is inside this particular interval. The truth is fixed — this interval either contains it or it does not. What is ninety-five percent is the procedure.
And the formula.
Estimate, plus or minus one point nine six times the standard error.
Hypothesis testing, four steps.

State the null — there is no relationship. Assume it is true. Ask how likely a relationship at least this big would be by sampling luck alone; that probability is the p-value. If p is below point zero five, reject the null. Otherwise you fail to reject it. You never accept it.
Type one and type two error.

Type one is a false positive — you announced something that is not there. The point zero five threshold caps that risk at five percent. Type two is a false negative, usually caused by too small a sample.
And then the distinction that costs the most points.

Statistically significant is not the same as important. Big samples make trivial effects significant — with three hundred thousand cases, a difference of a tenth of a point clears p below point zero five and means nothing.
The model case.

Levitt's capital punishment estimate. Even accepting the most generous deterrence numbers, executions explain about one point five percent of the nineteen nineties homicide decline. Real, arguably significant, and far too small to be the answer.
And significance says nothing about causality.
Nothing at all. A significant correlation still has to clear all four hurdles.
Correlation and regression. What do sign and size of r tell me?

Sign is direction, size is strength, and it runs from minus one to plus one. Two cautions. r equals zero means no straight-line relationship — a perfect U-shape has an r near zero. And r squared is the share of variation in Y that X accounts for.
Chocolate and Nobels.
r of zero point seven nine, so r squared of about zero point six two. Sixty-two percent of the variation. Impressive-sounding, and still not causal.
The sentence to write on the exam.
A one-unit increase in X is associated with a change of b units in Y. Associated with — not causes. And in a multiple regression, add: holding the other variables constant.
Quick significance check on a table.
If the coefficient is more than about twice its standard error, it is significant at p below point zero five.
Unit fourteen. King, Keohane and Verba give you one rule.
Select cases on the independent variable. Never on the dependent variable. Never on both.
What does selecting on Y do?
It biases your estimate toward zero. Keeping only high-Y cases cut an estimated slope from zero point six eight to zero point three two — it makes X look weaker than it is.
Is there a consolation?

One. Because the direction of the bias is known, a significant effect found in a truncated sample means the true effect is at least that large. Selecting on both X and Y is worse — the bias can run in any direction and you cannot know which.
The classic error.

No variation in Y is zero information. Study only revolutions and you cannot learn what causes revolutions, because you never see the countries with the same conditions that did not revolt. Same for studying only successful startups, only school shooters, only wars.
And selection rules you did not realise were selecting on Y.

Using only cases covered in newspapers. Only important cases. Only cases with available data. Only organisations that survived long enough to study. Any rule correlated with the outcome creates the bias.
And the Freakonomics pairing.

Venkatesh got a crack gang's actual financial records — an extraordinary source on a population nobody can survey, showing foot soldiers earning below minimum wage while the leader took a large share.
What can that do, and not do?
It can show a mechanism and kill a stereotype. It cannot establish a general causal claim — one non-randomly obtained case, no comparison group, no variation on the outcome.
Right. Trounstine's stated goal is that you can analyse, explain and apply to new contexts. So expect an unfamiliar claim and a request to evaluate it.

Five frames cover most of it. Frame one: here is a claim from the news, evaluate it. Run the four hurdles in order and say yes, no or maybe to each, with a reason. Name the specific confounder you are worried about, not other factors. Then finish with what evidence would settle it — usually an experiment that randomly assigned X — and explain why that is impossible here and what the next-best design would be.
Frame two.

Design a study to answer this question. State the hypothesis with a direction. Name the unit of analysis. Give an operational definition for X and Y and defend it against a validity objection. Say how you would assign or approximate assignment of X. Name your control group and what makes it a credible counterfactual. Then admit the biggest remaining threat to internal validity.
Frame three.

Why is this measure bad? Separate validity from reliability. Nobel prizes for cognitive function. No college degree for working class. Self-reported turnout for turnout. Then say which direction the error runs, because systematic error is far worse than noise.
Frame four.

This poll says X, how much should you trust it? Sampling error is the smallest error present. Ask about the frame, the response rate, the weighting, and the likely-voter screen. Cite Cohn's five-point spread from identical data, or Clinton's sixteen weightings. Recommend averaging polls, and note that averaging does not fix house effects.
And frame five.

Interpret this table or coefficient. Direction, size in real units, and whether it is significant — coefficient more than twice its standard error. Then say what it does not tell you. Add holding the other variables constant. And never write causes unless the design earns it.
Self-test. Twelve questions. Answer out loud, then listen for the answer.
One. Name the four hurdles, in order.

One, is there a credible causal mechanism connecting X to Y. Two, can we rule out that Y causes X. Three, is there covariation. Four, have we controlled for confounding variables Z. One confident no defeats the claim.
Two. What is the difference between random sampling and random assignment?

Random sampling picks who is in your study and buys external validity. Random assignment decides who gets the treatment and buys internal validity. A national survey has the first; a lab experiment on sixty undergraduates has the second.
Three. Why can you never directly measure a causal effect?

The fundamental problem of causal inference. A causal effect is the difference between what happened and what would have happened, but for any case you only ever observe one of those. Every method is a scheme for constructing a believable stand-in.
Four. A study finds counties with more churches have more crime. What is wrong?

Two things. Spuriousness — population size causes both, because bigger counties have more of everything. And the ecological fallacy — even if the county correlation were real, it says nothing about whether churchgoers commit crimes.
Five. A poll of a thousand has a plus or minus three point margin of error. What is that number covering?

Random sampling error only. Nothing about coverage error, nonresponse, response bias, question wording, weighting choices, or the likely-voter model. Those are usually larger, and none of them shrink when you interview more people.
Six. Why is no college degree a bad operational definition of working class?

It does not capture the concept. Forty percent of white non-college voters in two thousand four had family incomes over sixty thousand dollars, and more than half called themselves middle class. It is a validity failure, and swapping in income flips Bartels' answer.
Seven. You want to know what causes civil wars, so you study twenty civil wars. What is the error?
Selecting on the dependent variable, with no variation in Y. Every case has the same outcome, so nothing distinguishes causes from constants. Select on X, never on Y.
Eight. A result is significant at p below point zero zero one. Is it important?

Unknown. Significance answers whether it is probably not zero. With a large enough n a trivial difference clears any threshold. Levitt's capital punishment estimate explains about one point five percent of the crime decline.
Nine. What does a ninety-five percent confidence interval mean?

That the method captures the true value ninety-five percent of the time in repeated sampling. Not that there is a ninety-five percent chance the truth is inside this particular interval — the truth is fixed. Estimate plus or minus one point nine six standard errors.
Ten. Explain an antecedent variable versus an intervening variable.

An antecedent comes before X and causes both X and Y — spurious, and the claim dies. An intervening variable sits between X and Y and transmits the effect — the claim survives and is now explained. Same-looking diagram, opposite verdict.
Eleven. In the Gerber, Green and Larimer experiment, why four treatments instead of one?

To identify the mechanism. Civic duty plus one point eight, being studied plus two point five, your own record plus four point nine, your neighbours' records plus eight point one. The driver is not information or reminding — it is social surveillance.
Twelve. You have a strong correlation, r of zero point seven nine. Name three ways it could still be non-causal.

Reverse causation, where Y causes X. Spuriousness, where some Z causes both. And the ecological fallacy, where the correlation exists at the group level but not the individual level. Messerli's chocolate paper has all three at once.
That is the machinery. Before each quiz, read the relevant units and try the self-test cold.
Before the midterm and the final, do one pass through the four hurdles and one through the seven case files. Those two frames carry most of the points.
And when a new reading appears, ask the same three questions.
What is the claim. What is the comparison. And what would change my mind.
